html:
Gamla Uppsala, Old Uppsala, was the seat of the early kings of the Swedes and a great centre of the old Norse religion. Its three large royal burial mounds date from the 500s.

The German chronicler Adam of Bremen wrote about 1075 that a temple there held statues of Thor, Odin and Freyr, and that every nine years men and animals were sacrificed and hung in a sacred grove. Historians debate how much of this is true, but Uppsala was clearly the last stronghold of paganism in Scandinavia.

Christianity won out in the early 1100s, and a church was built on the site. In 1164 Uppsala became the seat of Sweden's archbishop, which later moved to the new town nearby. The mounds still stand. See Sweden and the Viking Age.
